title: Envy at the Ballot Box - Nautilus
gist: A European Economic Review study by Linköping University researchers finds that majority voting in groups makes people more willing to act out of envy than when they decide individually, using the Envy Game and Costly Envy Game experiments.

insights.claim: A study in the European Economic Review by Linköping University (Sweden) researchers found that when people vote as a group under majority rule, they are more inclined to act out of envy than when making the same decision individually.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Suggests that collective/majoritarian decision mechanisms (voting, board votes, shareholder resolutions) may systematically produce more spiteful or zero-sum outcomes than the same individuals would choose alone — a factor for modeling group governance and referendum outcomes.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "A recent paper in the European Economic Review"

insights.claim: Researchers tested subjects individually and in groups using two experimental designs: the Envy Game, where subjects chose between an even 40-40 split or an uneven 40-50 split favoring an anonymous peer at no personal cost, and the Costly (But Cheap) Envy Game, where the alternative to an even split was a 41-50 split that gave the subject a slight personal advantage.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: This experimental design isolates envy from self-interest, giving a reusable methodology for measuring how institutional context (voting vs. individual choice) shifts spiteful behavior even when it costs the actor nothing or very little.

insights.claim: In both experimental setups, choosing the option that gave the other person more money came at no immediate monetary disadvantage (Envy Game) or only a slight one (Costly Envy Game) to the decision-maker, isolating envy as the variable rather than material self-interest.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Because the cost of generosity was minimal, any drop in generosity under group voting versus individual choice can be attributed largely to social/psychological dynamics of voting itself, not economic rationality.
